minor_characters.name: Miss Norton
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A literary acquaintance in New York who hosts a salon and befriends Jo and Professor Bhaer during Jo’s boarding-house months.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her functions (a salon host, cultured friend) can be folded into Mrs. Kirke or unnamed 'friends,' without altering Jo’s New York arc or Bhaer’s defining scene.

minor_characters.name: Mr. Tudor
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A young Englishman in Nice who flirts and dances; chiefly a foil in Amy’s Riviera scenes.
minor_characters.reason_removable: He contributes no essential choice or turning point; Amy’s growth and courtship with Laurie proceed without his specific presence.

minor_characters.name: Miss Crocker
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A meddling Concord neighbor who appears in early social comic scenes.
minor_characters.reason_removable: She provides local color only, and her gossip/visits can be excised or generalized without affecting any core plot or theme.

minor_characters.name: Jenny Snow
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A schoolmate who tattles about Amy’s limes and spites her at a fair.
minor_characters.reason_removable: The humiliation and later magnanimity episodes can occur without naming a specific girl antagonist.

minor_characters.name: Mr. Davis
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Amy’s schoolmaster who punishes her for pickled limes in the classroom scene.
minor_characters.reason_removable: The episode in the synopsis (public humiliation over limes) can be narrated with an unnamed teacher without needing a recurring named figure.

minor_characters.name: The Chesters
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Society family who snub Amy around the charity fair and assign tables.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Amy’s ‘snubbed at a fair, answers with magnanimity’ beat works with an unnamed fashionable set; removing names trims clutter.

minor_characters.name: Mr. Scott
minor_characters.appearances_summary: John Brooke’s married neighbor whose household Meg and John sometimes visit in the domestic ‘newlyweds’ chapter.
minor_characters.reason_removable: He serves as a situational prop for Meg’s early-marriage learnings, which stand without his named presence.

minor_characters.name: Kitty and Minnie Kirke
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Mrs. Kirke’s little girls who swarm Jo and Professor Bhaer at the boardinghouse.
minor_characters.reason_removable: They add charm but no plot necessity; Jo’s and Bhaer’s rapport can be shown with Beth’s letters and adult conversations.

minor_characters.name: Tina
minor_characters.appearances_summary: The French ironing-woman’s child whom Professor Bhaer dotes on in New York.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her scenes showcase Bhaer’s tenderness but can be conveyed briefly or through Jo’s direct observation of his charity.

minor_characters.name: Frank Vaughn
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Fred Vaughn’s lame twin brother who accompanies Fred abroad and at Vevay.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Fred’s courtship beat is the only one the synopsis preserves; Frank’s presence adds texture but no decisions change by him.

minor_characters.name: Lady de Jones, the Serene Teuton, assorted nobles and hotel guests
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Comic European party-goers and titled bystanders in Amy/Laurie Riviera ball and hotel scenes.
minor_characters.reason_removable: These walk-ons are atmosphere only; Amy’s social setting and the ball’s function survive without them.

minor_characters.name: Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Early Boston hosts of the New Year’s dance where Jo meets Laurie.
minor_characters.reason_removable: The meeting can be staged at ‘a New Year’s dance’ without naming the Gardiners, saving space and names.

minor_characters.name: Mr. King and family
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Meg’s employer’s family (the Kings) during her governess post, including Grace and Ellen.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Meg’s ‘Vanity Fair’ lesson and Brooke courtship can be kept while compressing or anonymizing the employer family.

minor_characters.name: Miss Randal
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A passing New York lady whom Laurie jokingly cites as a flirtation.
minor_characters.reason_removable: She is a fleeting name used in banter and has no bearing on Jo’s or Laurie’s real choices.

minor_characters.name: Mr. Dashwood
minor_characters.appearances_summary: The ‘Weekly Volcano’ editor who buys Jo’s sensation stories and marks out her morals.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Jo’s ‘sensation stories’ arc can be summarized as ‘an editor’ without recurring scenes with a named gatekeeper.

minor_characters.name: Hannah Mullett
minor_characters.appearances_summary: The Marches’ outspoken housemaid who pops in with dialect humor, scolds, and domestic asides throughout home scenes.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her lines provide local color but no decisions or turns of plot depend on her specifically, and household business can be attributed to the sisters and Marmee.

minor_characters.name: Sallie Gardiner (later Mrs. Moffat)
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Society friend who hosts Meg at fashionable gatherings and reappears as a genial acquaintance after marriage.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Meg’s brush with fashion and its emptiness can occur at “a grand party” without naming or returning to Sallie.

minor_characters.name: Mrs. Moffat
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Sallie’s mother who fusses over Meg’s looks and social prospects during the party chapter.
minor_characters.reason_removable: She is an accessory to the same lesson about vanity and class that the scene already conveys without her as a distinct figure.

minor_characters.name: Ned Moffat
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A brief flirt and background young man around the Moffat party.
minor_characters.reason_removable: He neither advances Meg’s story nor meaningfully interacts with the main arcs beyond filler chatter.

minor_characters.name: Belle Moffat
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Another Moffat girl present in party scenes and social calls.
minor_characters.reason_removable: She adds crowd texture to society scenes that can be summarized without naming her.

minor_characters.name: Kate Vaughn
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A visiting young lady at Camp Laurence who talks manners and books with the March girls.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her cameo reinforces themes Jo and Amy learn elsewhere and can be cut without loss to relationships or plot.

minor_characters.name: Grace Vaughn
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Another Vaughn sibling seen in early visiting and picnic scenes.
minor_characters.reason_removable: She is background company and contributes nothing unique to the sisters’ growth.

minor_characters.name: Mrs. Chester
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A fashionable matron who presides over the charity fair where Amy is slighted.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Amy’s snub and gracious response can be shown without naming the hostess.

minor_characters.name: May Chester
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Mrs. Chester’s daughter who helps engineer the slight at the fair.
minor_characters.reason_removable: She is an interchangeable social rival whose specific identity is unimportant to the lesson.

minor_characters.name: Esther
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Aunt March’s devout maid who counsels Amy briefly during her stay.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Amy’s small self-mastery at Aunt March’s can be shown through Amy’s own reflections and Aunt March’s discipline without Esther.

minor_characters.name: Franz and Emil
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Bhaer’s nephews who appear among the first pupils at Plumfield and in the apple-picking scene.
minor_characters.reason_removable: They are part of the school’s crowd and need not be singled by name to establish Jo’s life work.

minor_characters.name: Tommy Bangs
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A mischievous Plumfield boy noted for sneaking “sweet-fern cigars” in bed.
minor_characters.reason_removable: He’s a color vignette whose mischief can be generalized as typical boyish scrapes at the school.

minor_characters.name: Flo (Florence) Carrol
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Aunt Carrol’s daughter who accompanies Amy abroad to London and Paris.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Amy’s letters, polish, and eventual meeting with Laurie abroad do not depend on Flo’s personality.

subplots.name: The home theatricals and ‘Operatic Tragedy’ performance
subplots.reason_removable: This long comic play-by-play is beloved flavor but not structurally required for any arc set by the synopsis.

subplots.name: The Pickwick Club newspaper and faux-Portfolio installments
subplots.reason_removable: The club itself can be mentioned in a line; printing its full mock ‘edition’ (ads, ode, cat-lament) slows the main story.

subplots.name: Meg’s lost glove and forged-note gossip at the Moffats
subplots.reason_removable: The courtship proceeds without the specific ‘glove in his pocket/forged note’ business; the ‘emptiness of fashion’ lesson suffices.

subplots.name: Meg’s neighborly ‘Scott supper’ detour
subplots.reason_removable: Her domestic-learning arc—scorched jelly, budget, and partnership with John—reads cleanly without this side visit.

subplots.name: Laurie’s glove-and-message pranks and petty jealousies
subplots.reason_removable: They offer comic friction but do not change the outcome of Jo’s refusal or Laurie’s growth in Europe.

subplots.name: Daisy and Demi’s extended ‘letter-gymnastics’ and nursery vignettes
subplots.reason_removable: These charming set pieces can be drastically compressed without harming the final harvest tableau in the synopsis.

subplots.name: Amy’s detailed Nice/Monaco society pageant
subplots.reason_removable: The ball, the lobster-luncheon fiasco, and her sensible flirt with Fred Vaughn can be retained while pruning the cameo-laden party tour.

subplots.name: Jo’s long salon-philosophy evening in New York
subplots.reason_removable: Bhaer’s moral fiber can be shown in one short exchange; the extended ‘philosophic pyrotechnics’ debate isn’t strictly necessary.

subplots.name: Extended Pickwick Portfolio readings and hedge post-office letters
subplots.reason_removable: The club’s existence and moral playfulness are preserved in brief while the many mock articles and letters can be drastically pruned without affecting arcs.

subplots.name: Home theatricals with the full “Operatic Tragedy” playlet
subplots.reason_removable: The fact of theatricals and neighborly bonding can stand with a line or two, so the page-long spoof script and stage directions can go.

subplots.name: The girls’ week of idleness and botched housekeeping (“Experiments”)
subplots.reason_removable: Its lesson about cheerful work and self-command is repeated elsewhere and can be summarized in a sentence.

subplots.name: Camp Laurence charades, croquet, and picnic games in detail
subplots.reason_removable: Relationship beats can be kept in passing while the elaborate charade-by-charade staging is dispensable.

subplots.name: Amy’s additional school squabbles beyond the limes episode
subplots.reason_removable: Her public humiliation over limes suffices to show her pride and correction without extra petty classroom rivalries.

subplots.name: Pages of formal social calling and name-catalogues during Amy’s and Jo’s “Calls”
subplots.reason_removable: The sisters’ lesson about true breeding can be conveyed without long lists of callers, cards, and etiquette minutiae.

subplots.name: Jo’s New York salon outings and literary parties with Miss Norton
subplots.reason_removable: Jo’s moral testing and course-correction are anchored in Bhaer’s influence and the Dashwood tales so the extra society cameos are optional.

subplots.name: Amy’s London season details before Switzerland (studio visits, dress and drive catalogues)
subplots.reason_removable: Her polish and tact are shown more decisively at the charity fair and in Switzerland with Laurie, making most London color expendable.

subplots.name: Laurie’s college antics, concerts, and prankish interludes
subplots.reason_removable: His maturation and feelings for Jo are clear without preserving every prank or performance vignette.

subplots.name: Meg’s assorted small domestic embarrassments beyond the jelly and ledger episodes
subplots.reason_removable: Her marriage-school arc is secured by the scorched jelly, blushes, and thrift ledger, so extra minor flusters can be cut.

digressions.topic: The Pickwick Portfolio (Anniversary Ode, Masked Marriage tale, cat-elegy, mock ads and hints)
digressions.reason_removable: These faux pages are playful meta-text that delay plot and can be summarized as ‘the sisters ran a home newspaper.’

digressions.topic: Full dramatic synopsis of ‘The Witch’s Curse’ home play
digressions.reason_removable: A brief mention of ‘home theatricals’ preserves character color without the multi-page skit transcript.

digressions.topic: Jo’s poem ‘A Song from the Suds’ inside the Letters chapter
digressions.reason_removable: The epistolary momentum holds without reproducing the entire poem; its sentiment can be folded into the letter’s prose.

digressions.topic: Jo’s full poem ‘In the Garret’ recited before the proposal
digressions.reason_removable: Its stanzas are touching but the scene’s turning point—Bhaer reading a verse that calls him—is preserved by excerpt or paraphrase.

digressions.topic: The pseudo-editorial/publishing minutiae with Mr. Dashwood marking out Jo’s morals
digressions.reason_removable: Line-edits and tariff talk on ‘sensation’ vs. ‘moral’ can be tightened to a single exchange without losing Jo’s artistic crisis.

digressions.topic: Extended pastoral catalogue of the apple-picking day’s scenery, flora, fauna, and boys’ romps
digressions.reason_removable: The culminating family gathering and toasts read the same if the scenic inventory is tightened to a line or two.

digressions.topic: Inventory of birthday gifts and comic food-play at the orchard tea
digressions.reason_removable: Abridging the item-by-item lists preserves the emotional beats (gratitude and family joy) without the enumerations.
